column1: # Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm wa-l-Ḥikam — Hadith 30: “Allah has laid down obligations”

column2: From Abū Thaʿlabah al-Khushanī (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: “Allah has laid down obligations, so do not neglect them; He has set limits, so do not transgress them; He has forbidden things, so do not violate them; and He has been silent about things, as a mercy to you and not out of forgetfulness, so do not search into them.”
A ḥasan hadith, reported by al-Dāraquṭnī and others.
This hadith comes through the narration of Makḥūl, from Abū Thaʿlabah al-Khushanī, and it has two defects.
First, Makḥūl's hearing from Abū Thaʿlabah is not authenticated; so said Abū Mushir al-Dimashqī, the ḥāfiẓ Abū Nuʿaym and others.

Second, it is disputed whether it is marfūʿ (attributed to the Prophet ﷺ) or mawqūf on Abū Thaʿlabah (his own words), and some reported it from Makḥūl as his own words. But al-Dāraquṭnī said: The marfūʿ version is more likely to be correct; and he said: It is better known.
The Shaykh (may Allah have mercy on him) graded this hadith ḥasan, and before him the ḥāfiẓ Abū Bakr ibn al-Samʿānī graded it ḥasan in his Amālī.

The meaning of this hadith has been narrated as marfūʿ by other routes. Al-Bazzār recorded it in his Musnad, as did al-Ḥākim, from the hadith of Abū al-Dardāʾ, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whatever Allah has made lawful in His Book is lawful,

whatever He has made unlawful is unlawful, and whatever He has been silent about is pardoned. So accept from Allah His leniency, for Allah would never forget anything.” Then he recited this verse: “And your Lord is never forgetful” [Maryam 19:64]. Al-Ḥākim said: Its chain is authentic; and al-Bazzār said: Its chain is fair (ṣāliḥ).

Al-Ṭabarānī and al-Dāraquṭnī recorded it by another route from Abū al-Dardāʾ, from the Prophet ﷺ, like the hadith of Abū Thaʿlabah, and he said at the end of it: “a mercy from Allah, so accept it”; but its chain is weak.

Al-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah recorded, through the narration of Sayf ibn Hārūn, from Sulaymān al-Taymī, from Abū ʿUthmān, from Salmān, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked about clarified butter, cheese and furs,
and he said: “The lawful is what Allah has made lawful in His Book, the unlawful is what Allah has made unlawful in His Book, and what He has been silent about is among what He has pardoned.”
Al-Tirmidhī said: Sufyān — meaning Ibn ʿUyaynah — reported it from Sulaymān, from Abū ʿUthmān, from Salmān as his own words. He said: And that seems more authentic.
In Kitāb al-ʿIlal he mentioned that al-Bukhārī said of the marfūʿ hadith: I do not think it is preserved. Aḥmad said: It is munkar; and Ibn Maʿīn also rejected it.
Abū Ḥātim al-Rāzī said: It is a mistake. The trustworthy narrators reported it from al-Taymī, from Abū ʿUthmān, from the Prophet ﷺ in mursal form, without Salmān in it.
I say: It has been narrated from Salmān as his own words by other routes.
Ibn ʿAdī recorded it from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar as marfūʿ and declared its chain weak.
Abū Ṣāliḥ al-Murrī reported it from al-Jurayrī, from Abū ʿUthmān al-Nahdī, from ʿĀʾishah as marfūʿ, and he erred in its chain.
It has also been narrated from al-Ḥasan in mursal form.

Abū Dāwūd recorded, from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: The people of the Jāhiliyyah used to eat some things and leave others out of distaste. Then Allah sent His Prophet ﷺ, sent down His Book, made lawful what He made lawful

and made unlawful what He made unlawful. So what He made lawful is lawful, what He made unlawful is unlawful, and what He was silent about is pardoned. And he recited: “Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden…” [al-Anʿām 6:145]. This is mawqūf.

ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr said: Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has made some things lawful and some unlawful. What He has made lawful is lawful, what He has made unlawful is unlawful, and what He has been silent about is pardoned.

In the hadith of Abū Thaʿlabah, then, he divided Allah's rulings into four categories: obligations, forbidden things, limits and what is passed over in silence; and that comprises all the rulings of the religion.

Abū Bakr ibn al-Samʿānī said: This hadith is one of the great foundations of the religion. He said: It is related that someone said: Among the hadiths of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ there is no single hadith that, on its own, brings together the roots and branches of knowledge more fully than the hadith of Abū Thaʿlabah.
He said: It is related that Abū Wāthilah al-Muzanī said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ gathered the religion into four phrases; and then he mentioned the hadith of Abū Thaʿlabah.
Ibn al-Samʿānī said: Whoever acts on this hadith has secured the reward and is safe from punishment,

because whoever fulfils the obligations, avoids the forbidden things, stops at the limits and refrains from searching into what has been kept from him has attained every kind of merit and fulfilled the rights of the religion;
for the laws do not go beyond these kinds mentioned in this hadith. End of quotation.
As for the obligations (farāʾiḍ), they are what Allah has made obligatory on His servants and required them to carry out, such as prayer, zakāh, fasting and Ḥajj.
The scholars have differed over whether wājib and farḍ, the two words for “obligatory”, mean the same thing or not.

Some said that they are the same, and that everything made obligatory by evidence from the Sharīʿah — the Book, the Sunnah, consensus or any other of the Sharīʿah's proofs — is farḍ. This is the well-known view of al-Shāfiʿī's followers and others, and it has been related as a reported position of Aḥmad,
because he said: Everything in the prayer is farḍ.
Others said: Rather, farḍ is what is established by conclusive evidence, and wājib what is established by evidence that is not conclusive. This is the view of the Ḥanafīs and others.

Most of Aḥmad's explicit statements distinguish farḍ from wājib. A number of his companions transmitted from him that he said: Nothing is called farḍ except what is in the Book of Allah the Exalted. And he said of the charity of breaking the fast (ṣadaqat al-fiṭr): I would not dare say that it is farḍ —
though he holds that it is wājib. Some of the scholars of our [Ḥanbalī] school said: He meant that farḍ is what is established by the Book, and wājib what is established by the Sunnah.

Others said: He meant that farḍ is what is established by widespread, mass-transmitted (mutawātir) report, and wājib what is established by independent reasoning (ijtihād), so that disagreement over its being obligatory is admissible.
A difficulty for this is that Aḥmad said, in al-Maymūnī's narration, of dutifulness to parents: It is not farḍ, but I say it is wājib, so long as it is not [a command to] disobedience.

Yet dutifulness to parents is agreed by consensus to be obligatory, and the commands to it in the Book and the Sunnah are many. The apparent sense of this is that he would not call anything farḍ except what the Book and the Sunnah have explicitly named farḍ.
The Salaf differed over enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong: is it to be called a farīḍah (an obligation) or not?
Juwaybir reported that al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: They are among the obligations of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; and the same has been narrated from Mālik.

ʿAbd al-Wāḥid ibn Zayd reported that al-Ḥasan said: It is not an obligation. It was an obligation on the Children of Israel, but Allah had mercy on this nation because of their weakness and made it voluntary for them.

ʿAbdullāh ibn Shubrumah wrote to ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd some well-known verses, the first of which is: “Enjoining what is right, ʿAmr, is a voluntary deed, / and those who undertake it are helpers of Allah.” Aḥmad's statements on it differ: is it to be called wājib or not?
A number of people reported from him what indicates that it is obligatory, while Abū Dāwūd reported from him, concerning a man who sees a lute (ṭunbūr) or the like: Is he obliged to change it?
He said: I do not know about “obliged”. If he changes it, that is a merit.

Isḥāq ibn Rāhawayh said: It is obligatory on every Muslim, unless he fears for himself. Perhaps Aḥmad hesitated to apply the word wājib to what is obligatory not on each individual but on the community as a whole.
The scholars have differed over jihād: is it obligatory or not?

A number of them denied that it is obligatory, among them ʿAṭāʾ, ʿAmr ibn Dīnār and Ibn Shubrumah; perhaps they meant this sense. Another group said it is obligatory, among them Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib and Makḥūl; perhaps the two of them meant that it is obligatory on the community.

Aḥmad said, in the narration of Ḥanbal: Going on campaign is obligatory on all people, as Ḥajj is obligatory; but if some of them go on campaign, that suffices for the rest. People cannot do without going on campaign.
Al-Marrūdhī asked him about jihād: Is it farḍ?

He said: They have differed over it, and it is not like Ḥajj. He meant that someone who is able to perform Ḥajj and has not done so is not released from it because others have performed it, whereas with jihād he is.
He was asked about the general call to arms (nafīr): when does it become obligatory?
He said: As for making it obligatory, I do not know; but if they fear for themselves, they must go out.

The apparent sense of this is that, out of scrupulousness, he hesitated to apply the word wājib to anything for which the texts do not use the language of obligation. In the same way he hesitated to apply the word ḥarām to what is disputed

and whose evidence from the texts of the Book or the Sunnah is conflicting. So he said of temporary marriage (mutʿah): I do not say it is ḥarām, but it is prohibited. He did not hesitate over the meaning of prohibition, but over applying its word,
because the texts and the Companions differ over it. This is the correct interpretation of Aḥmad's words.

He said of combining two sisters by right of possession: I do not say it is ḥarām, but it is prohibited. The correct interpretation of this is that he hesitated to apply the word ḥarām, not its meaning. All of this is by way of scrupulousness in speech,
for fear of falling under His words, Exalted is He: “Do not say, about what your tongues falsely describe, ‘This is lawful and this is unlawful,’ so as to invent lies against Allah” [al-Naḥl 16:116].

Al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym said: Let each of you beware of saying, “Allah has made such-and-such lawful and such-and-such unlawful,” and Allah saying: You lie; I did not make such-and-such lawful, nor such-and-such unlawful.
Ibn Wahb said: I heard Mālik ibn Anas say: I knew our scholars, and when one of them was asked, he would say, “I dislike this,” or “I do not like it”; they would not say “lawful” or “unlawful”.

As for what has been related of Aḥmad, that he said, “Everything in the prayer is farḍ”, that is not what he actually said. What his son ʿAbdullāh transmitted from him is that he said: Everything in the prayer that Allah has emphasised

is farḍ. This goes back to the sense of his saying that nothing is farḍ except what is in the Qurʾān; and what Allah has emphasised in the prayer is standing, recitation, bowing and prostration. Aḥmad said this only
because some people used to say: The prayer is farḍ, but bowing and prostration I do not say are farḍ; rather, they are Sunnah.
Mālik ibn Anas was asked about someone who says that, and he declared him a disbeliever. He was told: He is interpreting [the texts]. And he cursed him and said: He has said something grave.
Abū Bakr al-Naysābūrī transmitted this from him by several routes in his book Manāqib Mālik.

He also reported, with his chain, from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr ibn Maymūn ibn al-Rammāḥ, who said: I went in to Mālik ibn Anas and said: Abū ʿAbdillāh, what in the prayer is obligatory and what in it is Sunnah — or he said, voluntary?
Mālik said: The talk of heretics (zanādiqah)! Put him out.

Isḥāq ibn Manṣūr transmitted from Isḥāq ibn Rāhawayh that he rejected dividing the parts of the prayer into Sunnah and wājib, saying: Everything in the prayer is wājib; and he indicated that some of it requires the prayer to be repeated if it is omitted, and some does not.
The reason for this — and Allah knows best — is that calling something Sunnah may lead people to take it lightly, to lose interest in it and to leave it,

which is contrary to the Lawgiver's purpose of urging it and encouraging it by the means that lead to its being done and achieved. Using the word wājib is more likely to bring people to do it and to desire it.

The Lawgiver's speech does apply the word wājib to things whose omission, according to most scholars, is neither a sin nor punishable, such as the Friday bath, and likewise the guest's night, according to many or most of the scholars. What is meant by it is only to urge its performance strongly and to emphasise it.
As for the forbidden things (maḥārim), they are what Allah has fenced off, prohibiting anyone from approaching, committing or violating them.

The definitely forbidden things are mentioned in the Book and the Sunnah, as in His words, Exalted is He: “Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you: that you associate nothing with Him, be good to parents and not kill your children out of poverty…” [al-Anʿām 6:151], to the end of the three verses;

and His words, Exalted is He: “Say: My Lord has only forbidden indecencies, those open and those hidden, and sin, and transgression without right, and that you associate with Allah that for which He has sent down no authority, and that you say about Allah what you do not know” [al-Aʿrāf 7:33].
In some verses He mentions the things forbidden within a particular kind, as He mentions the forbidden foods in several places, among them His words, Exalted is He:

“Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to one who would eat it, unless it be carrion, blood poured forth or the flesh of swine — for that is filth — or a wicked thing dedicated to other than Allah” [al-Anʿām 6:145];

and His words: “He has only forbidden you carrion, blood, the flesh of swine and what has been dedicated to other than Allah” [al-Baqarah 2:173] — and in the other verse the same words come in a different order [al-Naḥl 16:115] — and His words:

“Forbidden to you are carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, what has been dedicated to other than Allah, the strangled, the beaten, the fallen, the gored, what a beast of prey has eaten — except what you slaughter — what has been sacrificed on stone altars, and seeking decisions by divining arrows” [al-Māʾidah 5:3].
He mentions the women forbidden in marriage in His words: “Forbidden to you are your mothers and your daughters…” [al-Nisāʾ 4:23].
He mentions the forbidden ways of earning in His words: “Allah has made trade lawful and usury (ribā) unlawful” [al-Baqarah 2:275].
As for the Sunnah, many forbidden things are mentioned in it, as in his saying ﷺ: “Allah has forbidden the sale of wine, carrion, swine and idols”;
his saying: “When Allah forbids something, He forbids its price”;
his saying: “Every intoxicant is unlawful”;
and his saying: “Your blood, your wealth and your honour are inviolable to one another.”
Whatever the Book and the Sunnah have explicitly declared unlawful, then, is forbidden.
Unlawfulness may also be inferred from a prohibition that is accompanied by a threat and by stern language, as in His words, the Mighty and Majestic:

“Wine, gambling, stone altars and divining arrows are only filth, of Satan's doing; so avoid it, that you may prosper. Satan only wants to stir up enmity and hatred between you through wine and gambling, and to turn you away from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer. Will you not then desist?” [al-Māʾidah 5:90–91].
As for a bare prohibition, people have differed over whether unlawfulness can be inferred from it.
It has been narrated that Ibn ʿUmar rejected inferring unlawfulness from it.
Ibn al-Mubārak said: Sallām ibn Abī Muṭīʿ informed us, from Ibn Abī Dakhīlah, from his father, who said: I was with Ibn ʿUmar, and he said:
The Messenger of Allah ﷺ prohibited raisins and dates — meaning that they be mixed [in steeping]. A man behind me said to me: What did he say?
I said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ made raisins and dates unlawful. ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar said: You lie. I said: Did you not say that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ prohibited it? Then it is unlawful.
He said: Will you bear witness to that?
Sallām said: It is as though he was saying that some of the Prophet's prohibitions ﷺ are matters of good manners.

We have mentioned above how scrupulous scholars such as Aḥmad and Mālik were wary of applying the word “unlawful” to what was not certainly unlawful, where there was some element of doubt or disagreement.

Al-Nakhaʿī said: They used to dislike things that they did not declare unlawful. Ibn ʿAwn said: Makḥūl said to me: What do you say about fruit that is thrown among the people and they scramble for it?
I said: Among us that is disliked. He said: Is it unlawful?
I said: Among us that is disliked. He said: Is it unlawful?
Ibn ʿAwn said: We found that harsh of Makḥūl.
Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad said: I heard a man ask al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad: Is singing unlawful?
Al-Qāsim was silent. Then he asked again, and he was silent; then he asked again, and al-Qāsim said to him: The unlawful is what is made unlawful in the Qurʾān.
Tell me: when truth and falsehood are brought before Allah, in which of them will singing be?
The man said: In falsehood. He said: Then give yourself the ruling.
ʿAbdullāh, the son of Imam Aḥmad, said: I heard my father say: Of the things the Prophet ﷺ prohibited, some are unlawful, as in his words:

“He prohibited that a woman be married together with her paternal aunt or her maternal aunt”; this is unlawful. And he prohibited the skins of beasts of prey; this is unlawful. And he mentioned other things of this kind.
Others among the things he prohibited are matters of good manners.
As for the limits of Allah, which He prohibited transgressing, what is meant by them is the whole of what He has permitted to be done, whether as obligatory, recommended or permissible;

and transgressing them is going beyond that into committing what He has prohibited, as the Exalted says: “Those are the limits of Allah, and whoever transgresses the limits of Allah has wronged himself” [al-Ṭalāq 65:1]. What is meant is

one who divorces in a way other than what Allah has commanded and permitted. The Exalted also says: “Those are the limits of Allah, so do not transgress them; and whoever transgresses the limits of Allah — it is they who are the wrongdoers” [al-Baqarah 2:229]. What is meant is
one who, after divorcing, keeps his wife without kindness or releases her without grace, or takes back some of what he gave the woman other than by way of the ransom Allah has permitted.

The Exalted also says: “Those are the limits of Allah; whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, He will admit him to gardens…” up to His words: “And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger and transgresses His limits, He will admit him to a Fire, abiding in it for ever, and he will have a humiliating punishment” [al-Nisāʾ 4:13–14]. What is meant is one who goes beyond what Allah has prescribed for the heirs,

favouring one heir by giving him more than his due, or giving him less than it. That is why the Prophet ﷺ said in his sermon at the Farewell Ḥajj: “Allah has given everyone with a right his right, so there is no bequest to an heir.”
Al-Nawwās ibn Samʿān reported that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Allah has struck a parable: a straight path, with two walls on either side of the path, in which are open doors,

with curtains hanging over the doors. At the entrance of the path there is a caller saying: O people, enter the path, all of you, and do not turn aside. And there is a caller calling from within the path;

whenever someone wants to open any of those doors, he says: Woe to you, do not open it, for if you open it you will go through it. The path is Islam, the two walls are the limits of Allah, the open doors are the things Allah has forbidden,

the caller at the head of the path is the Book of Allah, and the caller from above is Allah's admonisher in the heart of every Muslim.” Imam Aḥmad recorded it, and this is his wording; al-Nasāʾī recorded it in his Tafsīr, and al-Tirmidhī, who graded it ḥasan.
In this hadith the Prophet ﷺ likened Islam to a straight path: a smooth, wide road that brings the one who travels it to what he seeks, and which, besides that, is straight,

without crookedness, which makes it short and easy. On either side of the path, to the right and the left, are two walls, which are the limits of Allah. Just as a wall stops whoever is inside it from crossing it and going beyond it,

so Islam stops whoever has entered it from leaving its limits and going beyond them. Beyond the bounds Allah has set to what is permitted there is nothing but what He has prohibited. That is why He, Glorified is He, has praised those who keep His limits,

and censured whoever does not know the boundary between the lawful and the unlawful, as the Exalted says: “The Bedouins are more severe in disbelief and hypocrisy, and more likely not to know the limits of what Allah has sent down to His Messenger” [al-Tawbah 9:97].
The hadith about the Qurʾān has already been given: that it says of one who acted on it, He kept my limits, and of one who did not act on it, He transgressed my limits.

What is meant is that whoever does not go beyond what he has been permitted into what he has been prohibited has kept the limits of Allah, and whoever goes beyond that has transgressed the limits of Allah.

“Limits” (ḥudūd) is sometimes used to mean the forbidden things themselves, and then one says: Do not approach the limits of Allah, as the Exalted says: “Those are the limits of Allah, so do not approach them” [al-Baqarah 2:187]. What is meant is the prohibition of committing the things the verse forbids during the fast and during spiritual retreat (iʿtikāf) in the mosques.

Of this sense — calling the forbidden things limits — is the Prophet's saying ﷺ: “The likeness of the one who upholds the limits of Allah and the one who compromises over them is that of a people who divided up a ship among themselves…” — the well-known hadith. By the one who upholds the limits of Allah he meant the one who rejects forbidden things and prohibits them.
In the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās, the Prophet ﷺ said: “I am holding you by your waist-wrappers, saying: Guard yourselves against the Fire! Guard yourselves against the limits!” He said it three times.

Al-Ṭabarānī and al-Bazzār recorded it. By the limits he meant the things Allah has forbidden and acts of disobedience to Him. Of this kind too is the saying of the man who said to the Prophet ﷺ: I have committed a ḥadd, so carry it out on me.

The fixed punishments that deter people from grave forbidden acts are also called ḥudūd, as one says: the ḥadd for fornication, the ḥadd for theft, the ḥadd for drinking wine. Of this is the Prophet's saying ﷺ to Usāmah: “Do you intercede concerning one of the ḥudūd of Allah?” — meaning amputation for theft.
This is the well-known meaning of the term ḥudūd in the jurists' usage.
As for the Prophet's saying ﷺ, “No one is to be given more than ten lashes except in one of the ḥudūd of Allah,” people have differed over its meaning.
Some took ḥudūd here to mean these fixed punishments, and said that discretionary punishment (taʿzīr) may not go beyond ten lashes,
and that this number may be exceeded only in these fixed punishments. Others took ḥudūd here to mean the forbidden things of Allah in general, and said:

What is meant is that going beyond ten lashes is permitted only for committing one of the forbidden things of Allah; as for a beating to discipline someone for something not forbidden, it does not go beyond ten lashes.

Someone has taken his words ﷺ, “He has set limits, so do not transgress them,” to refer to these punishments that deter from forbidden things, saying that what is meant is the prohibition of going beyond these ḥudūd and exceeding them when carrying them out on criminals.

He supported this by saying that if “limits” meant stopping at the commands and prohibitions, it would repeat his words, “He has laid down obligations, so do not neglect them … He has forbidden things, so do not violate them.” But the matter is not as he said,

for stopping at the limits means not leaving what has been permitted for what has been prohibited, and that covers the permitted whether it is obligatory, recommended or permissible, as was said above. So there is no repetition in this hadith. And Allah knows best.

As for what is passed over in silence, it is that whose ruling has not been mentioned, whether as lawful, obligatory or unlawful; so it is pardoned, and there is no blame on the one who does it. This is what these hadiths mentioned here indicate, such as the hadith of Abū Thaʿlabah and others.

The wordings of the hadith of Abū Thaʿlabah differ. It has been narrated with the wording given above, and also with another: “Allah has laid down obligations, so do not neglect them; He has prohibited you from things, so do not violate them; and He has pardoned things, not out of forgetfulness, so do not search into them.” Isḥāq ibn Rāhawayh recorded it.

It has been narrated with yet another wording: “Allah has laid down obligations, so do not neglect them; He has instituted practices (sunan) for you, so do not violate them; He has forbidden you things, so do not transgress them; and He has left things between these, not out of forgetfulness but as a mercy from Him, so accept them and do not search into them.” Al-Ṭabarānī recorded it.
This narration makes clear that what is pardoned is what has been left unmentioned, so that it has been neither made unlawful nor made lawful.

But it should be known that a thing's being mentioned as unlawful or lawful may be hard to grasp from the texts of the Book and the Sunnah. For these texts may indicate it explicitly and plainly, or by way of generality and inclusion,

or by way of implication and intimation, as in His words, Exalted is He: “Do not say ‘Uff!’ to them” [al-Isrāʾ 17:23]; for kinds of harm greater than saying “uff” are included a fortiori. This is called the implication of agreement (mafhūm al-muwāfaqah).

Or they may indicate it by way of the contrary implication (mafhūm al-mukhālafah), as in his words, “On grazing sheep there is zakāh,” which by its implication shows that there is no zakāh on sheep that are not grazing. Most scholars have adopted this, giving weight to the contrary implication and treating it as a proof.
Or they may indicate it by way of analogy. When the Lawgiver states a ruling on something for a certain reason, and that reason is found in something else,

the ruling extends, according to the majority of scholars, to everything in which that reason is found. This belongs to the justice and the balance that Allah sent down and commanded us to use as a measure. All of this is a means by which the texts' indication of lawfulness and unlawfulness is known.
Where all of that is absent, the fact that something is not mentioned as obligatory or unlawful is taken as evidence that it is pardoned. Here there are two approaches.

The first is to say: There is no obligation and no prohibition except by the Sharīʿah; the Sharīʿah has not made such-and-such obligatory, or has not made it unlawful; so it is not obligatory, or not unlawful. This is how it is argued that the witr prayer and the sacrifice (uḍḥiyah) are not obligatory, or that the lizard (ḍabb) and the like are not unlawful,

or that certain disputed contracts, such as watering contracts (musāqāh) and sharecropping (muzāraʿah), are not unlawful. This goes back to presuming the continuance of freedom from liability where nothing is found to indicate that one is liable. This argument is valid only for someone who knows the kinds of evidence in the Sharīʿah and has examined them thoroughly.

If, in addition, he is certain that there is nothing to indicate obligation or prohibition, he is certain that there is no obligation or prohibition, as one is certain that there is no obligation of a sixth prayer, or of fasting a month other than Ramaḍān,

or of zakāh on wealth other than the zakatable kinds, or of a Ḥajj other than the Ḥajj of Islam — even though all of this is also proved by texts stating it explicitly. And if he thinks it likely that there is nothing to indicate obligation or prohibition, he thinks it likely, without certainty, that there is no obligation or prohibition.
The second approach is to cite general evidence of the Sharīʿah indicating that whatever the Sharīʿah has not made obligatory or unlawful is pardoned,
such as this hadith of Abū Thaʿlabah and the hadiths of similar meaning mentioned with it, and such as his saying ﷺ when he was asked whether the Ḥajj was to be every year:

“Leave me as long as I leave you. Those before you were destroyed only by their many questions and their disagreeing with their prophets. So when I prohibit you from something, avoid it, and when I command you to do something, do of it what you can.”

And such as his saying ﷺ in the hadith of Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ: “The Muslim who has committed the greatest crime against the Muslims is one who asked about something that had not been made unlawful, and it was made unlawful because of his asking.”

The Qurʾān too has indicated something like this in several places, as in His words, the Mighty and Majestic: “Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to one who would eat it, unless it be carrion…” [al-Anʿām 6:145],

which shows that whatever he did not find to be forbidden is not forbidden; and likewise His words: “What is the matter with you that you do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has been mentioned, when He has explained to you in detail what He has forbidden you, except what you are compelled to?” [al-Anʿām 6:119].

So He rebuked them for not eating of what Allah's name had been mentioned over, giving as the reason that He had made the unlawful clear to them and this was not part of it. This shows that things are permissible [by default];
otherwise He would not have blamed those who refrained from eating what had not been stated to be lawful for them merely because it had not been stated to be unlawful.
Know that this question is not the same as the question of the ruling on things before the coming of revelation: is it prohibition, permission, or no ruling at all?

For that question concerns the time before the coming of revelation. After it came, these texts and others like them have shown that the ruling of that original state has been removed, and it has become settled, by the proofs of the Sharīʿah, that the default ruling on things is permissibility.
Some have related a consensus on this, and judged mistaken those who treated the two questions as the same and gave them one ruling.
Imam Aḥmad's words indicate that whatever does not fall within the texts of prohibition is pardoned.
Abū al-Ḥārith said: I said to Abū ʿAbdillāh — meaning Aḥmad: The bird-catchers slaughter birds we do not recognise; what do you think of eating them?

He said: There is no harm in any bird that does not have a talon or eat carrion. So he confined the prohibition of birds to those with talons, which is stated in the texts, and those that eat carrion,
since they are in the same case as the crow, which is stated in the texts; and he judged everything else permissible.

The hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās mentioned above indicates the same, and the hadith of Salmān al-Fārisī contains the prohibition of asking about cheese, clarified butter and furs. Cheese used to be made in the land of the Magians and other disbelievers like them,

and so was clarified butter, and furs were likewise imported from them; and their slaughtered animals are carrion. This is one of the arguments for the permissibility of the milk and rennet of carrion, and of the permissibility of the Magians' food,

on all of which there is a well-known disagreement. The hadith is understood to mean that when the matter is uncertain, asking and searching into it are not obligatory, as Ibn ʿUmar said when he was asked about cheese made by the Magians:

What I find in the Muslims' market I buy, and I do not ask about it. Cheese was mentioned in the presence of ʿUmar, and he was told that it was made with rennet from carrion, and he said: Mention Allah's name and eat.
Imam Aḥmad said: The most authentic hadith on it is this hadith — meaning the one about the cheese of the Magians.
It has been narrated, from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās, that the Prophet ﷺ was brought a cheese during the expedition of al-Ṭāʾif and said: “Where is this made?”
They said: In Persia. He ﷺ said: “Put the knife in it and cut, mention the name of Allah and eat.” Imam Aḥmad recorded it. He was asked about it and said:
It is a munkar hadith. Abū Ḥātim al-Rāzī said the same.
Abū Dāwūd recorded its meaning from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, except that he said: during the expedition of Tabūk. Abū Ḥātim said: It too is munkar.
ʿAbd al-Razzāq recorded it in his book in mursal form, which is more likely, and his version has an addition: He was asked: Messenger of Allah, we fear it may be carrion.
He said: “Mention Allah's name over it and eat it.”
Al-Ṭabarānī recorded its meaning from the hadith of Maymūnah. Its chain is sound, but it is very unusual (gharīb).
In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, from ʿĀʾishah: Some people said to the Prophet ﷺ: People bring us meat, and we do not know whether the name of Allah was mentioned over it or not.
He said: “Mention the name of Allah over it yourselves and eat.” She said: They had only recently left disbelief.
In the Musnad of Imam Aḥmad, from al-Ḥasan: ʿUmar wanted to prohibit garments of striped Yemeni cloth (ḥibarah),
because they were dyed with urine. Ubayy said to him: That is not for you to do. The Prophet ﷺ wore them, and we wore them in his time. Al-Khallāl recorded it by another route, and in his version:

Ubayy said to him: Commander of the Believers, the Prophet of Allah ﷺ wore them, and Allah saw where they were; had Allah known that they were unlawful, He would have prohibited them. He said: You are right.

Imam Aḥmad was asked about wearing what the People of the Book dye, without washing it. He said: Why do you ask about what you do not know? People, for as long as we have known them, have never objected to that.

He was asked about Jews who dye with urine, and he said: The Muslim and the disbeliever are the same in this. Do not ask about this or search into it. And he said: If you know that it is definitely dyed with some urine, and you are sure of it, then do not pray in it until you have washed it.

He recorded, from the hadith of al-Mughīrah ibn Shuʿbah, that the Prophet ﷺ was given a pair of leather socks as a gift and wore them without knowing whether they came from a properly slaughtered animal or not.
There are also reports that are cited as evidence for searching and asking. Imam Aḥmad recorded, from the hadith of a man, from Umm Muslim al-Ashjaʿiyyah,
that the Prophet ﷺ came to her while she was in a leather tent and said: “How fine it is, if there is no carrion in it!” She said: So I began going over it. The man is unknown.

Al-Athram recorded, with his chain, from Zayd ibn Wahb, who said: A letter from ʿUmar reached us in Azerbaijan: You are in a land where there is carrion, so do not wear furs until you know which are lawful and which are not.
Al-Khallāl reported, with his chain, from Mujāhid, that Ibn ʿUmar saw a fur on a man, touched it and said: If I knew it was from a slaughtered animal, I would be glad to have a garment of it.
From Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb: he said to ʿĀʾishah: What keeps you from taking a quilt of fur?
She said: I dislike wearing carrion.

ʿAbd al-Razzāq reported, with his chain, from Ibn Masʿūd, that he said to the Muslims who had settled in Persia: When you buy meat, ask; if it was slaughtered by a Jew or a Christian, eat it. This was because most of the people of Persia were Magians, whose slaughtered animals are unlawful.

The disagreement on this resembles the disagreement over the permissibility of the food of those disbelievers whose slaughtered animals are not permitted, and over using the vessels and clothes of the idolaters;

and the disagreement over these goes back to the principle of what to do when the original state and the apparent state conflict. This was discussed in the commentary on the hadith, “The lawful is clear and the unlawful is clear, and between them are doubtful matters.”
His words about the things He was silent about, “as a mercy, not out of forgetfulness”, mean that He was silent about mentioning them only out of mercy and kindness to His servants,

in that He did not make them unlawful for them so as to punish them for doing them, nor obligatory on them so as to punish them for leaving them, but made them pardoned: if they do them, there is no blame on them,

and if they leave them, likewise. In the hadith of Abū al-Dardāʾ: Then he recited: “And your Lord is never forgetful” [Maryam 19:64]. Similar to it are His words, the Mighty and Majestic: “My Lord neither errs nor forgets” [Ṭā Hā 20:52].
His words, “so do not search into them”, may mean that this prohibition was particular to the time of the Prophet ﷺ,

because much searching and questioning about what had not been mentioned could cause stringency to be sent down about it, through obligation or prohibition; the hadith of Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ indicates this. Or the prohibition may be general,

as is indicated by what is narrated from Salmān as his own words. For much searching and questioning about the ruling on something not mentioned among the obligations or the prohibitions may lead one to believe it unlawful or obligatory,

because it resembles some obligatory or unlawful things. So accepting the leniency in it and refraining from searching and asking about it is better. This may come under the Prophet's saying ﷺ, “Ruined are those who go to extremes (al-mutanaṭṭiʿūn),” which he said three times.

Muslim recorded it from the hadith of Ibn Masʿūd as marfūʿ. The mutanaṭṭiʿ is one who delves deeply and probes into what does not concern him. This may be seized upon by those who cling to the outward wording and deny meanings and analogy, such as the Ẓāhirīs.
The precise position on this point — and Allah knows best — is that searching into what has no specific or general text about it is of two kinds.

The first is to examine whether it falls within what the authentic texts indicate by implication, inference and clear, sound analogy. This is right, and it is something those who exercise independent reasoning must do to know the rulings of the Sharīʿah.

The second is that the inquirer scrutinises far-fetched distinctions with minute attention, and so distinguishes between two like things merely on the basis of a difference that has no evident effect in the Sharīʿah,

although the attributes that call for treating them alike are present; or treats two different things alike merely on the basis of coincidental attributes that are not relevant and that no evidence shows to have any effect in the Sharīʿah.

This kind of inquiry and searching is neither approved nor praiseworthy, though groups of jurists have fallen into it. What is praiseworthy is only inquiry that agrees with the inquiry of the Companions and of those after them in the favoured generations, such as Ibn ʿAbbās and others like him.

Perhaps this is what Ibn Masʿūd meant by saying: Beware of going to extremes, beware of delving too deep, and keep to the old way — meaning the way the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) followed.

One of the Shāfiʿī imams said: It does not befit us to be content with fancies when drawing distinctions, as is the habit of the people of opinion (ahl al-raʾy). The reason is that rulings, as matters now stand, turn on probabilities and on what is most probable.

So when two questions are more probably alike than different, they must be judged alike, even if some remote difference suggests itself. Understand this, for it is one of the rules of the religion. End of quotation.

Among what falls under the prohibition of delving too deep and searching are the matters of the unseen that are reported to us, which we are commanded to believe in without their modality being explained. Some of them may have no counterpart in this perceptible world,
so searching into how they are is among what does not concern one; it is prohibited, and it may lead to bewilderment and doubt, and rise to the point of denial.
In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Abū Hurayrah, the Prophet ﷺ said: “People will keep asking until it is said: This is Allah, who created creation; then who created Allah?

Whoever finds anything of that, let him say: I believe in Allah.” In another narration of his: “People will keep asking you about knowledge until they say: This is Allah, who created us; then who created Allah?”
And in another narration of his:
“People will ask you about everything, until they say: Allah created everything; then who created Him?”
Al-Bukhārī recorded it, with the wording: “Satan comes to one of you and says: Who created such-and-such?
Who created such-and-such?
until he says: Who created your Lord?
When it reaches that, let him seek refuge with Allah and stop.”

In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Anas, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: Your nation will keep saying, What is this? What is that? until they say: This is Allah, who created creation; then who created Allah?”
Al-Bukhārī recorded it, with the wording: “People will not cease asking one another: This is Allah, the Creator of everything; then who created Allah?”
Isḥāq ibn Rāhawayh said: It is not permitted to think about the Creator. The servants may think about created things, according to what they have heard about them, but they should not go beyond that,

because if they do, they will lose their way. He said: Allah has said: “There is nothing but glorifies Him with His praise” [al-Isrāʾ 17:44]. So it may not be said: How do bowls, tables, baked bread and woven clothes glorify Him?
Knowledge that all of these glorify Him is sound; and it is for Allah to make their glorification however He wills and as He wills. People may not delve into that except with what they know,

and they should not speak on this and things like it except with what Allah has told, and should not go beyond that. So fear Allah, and do not delve into these ambiguous matters, for delving into them will bring you down from the path of truth.
Ḥarb transmitted all of this from Isḥāq (may Allah have mercy on him).
